title: Nachmanides
hookLine: a Catalan rabbi who defended Judaism at the Barcelona disputation, then settled in the land of Israel

cards: Rambam, yesterday. Ramban, today. One letter changes, and it's a different man, born about two generations later, in a different country.
Moshe ben Maimon became the Rambam. Moshe ben Nachman became the Ramban, and in English, Nachmanides.
He lived in Girona, in Catalonia, a doctor and a rabbi, and he wrote a commentary on the Torah that is still printed in study editions today. Then a summons came.

The king of Aragon wanted him in Barcelona, in the royal palace, to answer questions about his faith in public, against a man who had been born Jewish and become a Christian friar. He could not refuse.

teach.b: The debate is called the Barcelona disputation. The friar, Pablo Christiani, argued that passages in the rabbis' own writings showed the messiah had already come.
The Ramban was asked to respond, in front of the king and church leaders. Picture the risk: a rabbi speaking freely about another faith, before the powerful, could put his whole community in danger.
So before he began, by his own account, he asked the king for one thing: permission to speak freely. The king granted it. What we know comes mostly from the Ramban's own written report.
There's also a short Latin record from the other side, and the two don't tell it the same way; each side wrote down its own version. What stands out in the Ramban's account is his manner.

teach.h: POINT BY POINT, FROM THE TEXTS.
teach.b: He answers point by point, from the texts. He says the stories in the Talmud and the midrash are not all binding in the same way as law.
He is direct, at times sharp, and respectful of the king, who, he writes, sent him home with a gift. Afterward his account was published, and he faced trouble for it.
In time he left Catalonia and made the journey to the land of Israel.
In a letter home to his son, he describes Jerusalem as poor and desolate, and tells how he helped gather a few people and set up a place to pray. Strength of argument, without contempt.
And when the pressure grew, a new beginning far away.

how: The Ramban's Torah commentary is printed in study editions of the Bible alongside Rashi and Ibn Ezra, and a synagogue in Jerusalem's Old City bears his name.

games.q: you are the Ramban, summoned to answer about your faith before the king. one wrong word could endanger your community. what do you ask for first?
o: a promise that you will be declared the winner.
games.why: by his own account he asked the king for freedom to speak, and then answered point by point from the texts.

practice: Think of one conversation coming up where you'll need to hold your ground, at work, at home, online, and before the words, find the manner.
What's the one thing you want to say clearly, and the one thing you won't say, because it would only wound? If you pray, you can ask in your own words for a steady voice.

wordCard.voice: Ramban. Rabbi Moshe ben Nachman, called Nachmanides: a Torah commentator from Girona who answered in public at Barcelona, then went to Jerusalem. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: defend with dignity. The Ramban asked to speak freely, then spoke with care. See you tomorrow.
